name: Ivan Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work nights at Northgate Plastics, on an injection moulding press. That's a machine that squirts hot plastic into a steel mould and pops out a part, in my case door clips and little trim pieces for cars. I clock in at ten, check the hopper's full of pellets, watch the parts drop, trim the flash off with a knife and pack them in boxes of five hundred. Most nights it's fine, but around four in the morning your eyes go and that's when I make mistakes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What kind of mistakes, and what happens when you make one?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Short shots, mostly, where the mould doesn't fill and the clip comes out with a bit missing. If I don't catch it, a whole box goes back from the customer and it's on my name. I had a written warning in September for my scrap rate, so I'm still a bit on probation in my own head. Dennis, the setter who's been there thirty years, says everyone's rubbish for the first two years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how are things money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My girlfriend Kasia and me rent a flat above a launderette on Station Road. She's a care worker, does home visits, so between nights and her early starts we pass each other on the stairs. We've got about three months of bills put by, which took us two years. The rent went up again in the summer and that's what we actually talk about at the kitchen table, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Every few months the bosses wave some new system at us and it ends up being a screen nobody looks at. At the union meeting I'd say good, now let's talk about the night shift allowance instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job stays my job, which is a relief. But my problems don't go anywhere, because the rent's still climbing and my scrap rate is still on a sheet in the office. Nothing in this picture fixes nights or the warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and keep my head down until the warning drops off my record next March. I'd push the union to fight for a better night rate in the spring pay round. Kasia and me would keep putting a bit by each month, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, but not calm, if that makes sense. I still lie awake some mornings doing sums in my head about the rent. AI going nowhere just means the worries stay the ordinary ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the rent is what you talk about at the kitchen table. What would you do if it went up again next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd look further out, maybe past the ring road where it's cheaper, but then I need a car for nights because there's no bus at ten. A car eats the savings. So probably we'd just grit our teeth and pay it and cut the takeaways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the routine tasks get automated, which bit of your shift could that touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the counting and the labels on the boxes, that's already half done by a scale. Shirin in the office does the paperwork, so that would hit her more than me. My bit is hands and eyes, and nobody's showed me a computer that can trim flash with a knife.

say: I'd tell people the AI talk was **hype** all along, like every other new system.
I'd tell the union meeting to focus on the **night shift allowance** instead.
think: I'm relieved my **job stays mine**, but the rent and my warning don't go away.
The small automation lands on **office paperwork**, like Shirin's job, more than on my press.
do: Keep my head down until the **written warning** drops off next March.
Push the union for a better **night rate** in the spring pay round.
Keep saving a bit each month with Kasia, as we do **now**.
feel: **Mostly fine** about work, but still lying awake doing sums about the **rent**.
S0.quote: AI going nowhere just means the worries stay the ordinary ones.
fieldNote: His real pressures are **rent** and a **scrap-rate warning**, not technology.
He frames everything through the **union**, even in the calmest picture.
He notices the office worker Shirin would be hit before him, which shows **solidarity** rather than relief.

steps.text: Keep working nights quietly until the scrap warning clears in March
Raise the night shift allowance at the spring union meeting
Keep putting a little into the joint savings pot each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the union always says: if the company gets richer from this, the people on the floor should get a cut. I'd say it loudly at the canteen table. Online I don't really post, Kasia does that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the robots coming slower is the only bit that saves me. We've already got one robot arm on press six, and my old workmate Dennis says there used to be two people on that press. If the office side gets cheaper with AI, the money they save goes into more arms like that, not into my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting instead of half of them, and I'd ask the rep straight out what the plan is for press six. I'd stop eating out and try to push the savings from three months to five. I wouldn't do some computer course, because I'd be the slowest one in the room and I'd quit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, a bit. It's like watching the water come up slowly while everyone tells you it's only up to your ankles. I don't like changing things, so I'd rather the floor just stayed the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't do a computer course. Is there anything you would learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A forklift ticket, maybe, because that's still driving a thing with your hands. Dennis did his years ago and he says it got him out of two layoffs. That's about as far as I'd stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shirin in the office, because buying and planning is exactly the stuff on your card. And Dennis, because he's sixty-one and he'd never get another job if they pushed him. The young ones like me can at least go stack shelves somewhere.

say: I'd say the people on the **floor** deserve a cut of whatever the company saves.
I'd say it at the **canteen table**, not online, because Kasia does the posting.
think: I think the **slow robots** are the only thing protecting my press.
I expect office savings to pay for more **robot arms**, like the one on press six, not wages.
do: Attend every **union meeting** and ask the rep about plans for press six.
Cut eating out to push savings from **three to five months**.
Look into a **forklift licence** rather than any computer course.
feel: A **tight chest**, like watching water rise while being told it's only ankle deep.
Uncomfortable with **change** and wishing the floor would just stay the floor.
S1.quote: We've already got one robot arm on press six, and my old workmate Dennis says there used to be two people on that press.
fieldNote: He sees the risk through a robot arm already on **press six**, not through the news.
He refuses screen-based **training** because he expects to fail, not because he thinks it's useless.
His worry for older colleague **Dennis** is stronger than his worry for himself.

steps.text: Ask the union rep directly what happens to press six workers
Stop eating out to grow savings from three to five months
Book a forklift licence course, the way Dennis did years ago

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice somebody's making, not the weather. Governments could tax the machines and keep people in work, and I'd say that at the union, at the pub, anywhere. I'd probably even sign petitions, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means by the time I'm thirty-two there's a robot doing my press, and I'm a guy with a school certificate and a forklift ticket at best. The thinking AI in 2028 takes Shirin's job and the planner's job first, so I'd watch it happen to them and know I'm next. Three years isn't long enough for someone like me to become something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending anything I didn't have to and get the savings up as high as they'll go before 2031. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd vote for whoever promised to slow it down or pay people when it lands. In the first year after the robots, I'd probably be leaning on Kasia's wage and on whatever help the government puts up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. My dad was out of work for two years when the steelworks shut. I don't want to be sitting in the kitchen like my dad at thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on Kasia's wage. Is her job safe in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Care work is the last thing anyone wants a robot doing, so maybe she'd be alright for a bit longer. But one care worker's wage won't pay the rent on Station Road. We'd have to move somewhere smaller or in with her mother, which neither of us wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of your job that changes in 2028, before the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The scheduling and the quality reports would go to the computer, so the supervisors shrink first. That might make the floor even tighter, with one supervisor for three lines and less slack for someone with my scrap rate. So even before 2031, I'd be the one they look at first.

say: I'd say it's a **choice** governments are making, and they could tax the machines.
I'd sign **petitions** and talk about it at the union and the pub, which I never do.
think: I think a robot runs my press by **2031**, when I'm thirty-two.
I'd watch thinking AI take the **office jobs** first in 2028 and know I'm next.
Three years isn't long enough for someone like me to **retrain**.
do: Cut all spending now and push **savings** as high as possible before 2031.
Vote and campaign for whoever promises to **slow it down** or pay people.
Lean on Kasia's **wage** and government help in the first year after robots.
feel: **Sick**, remembering his dad sitting in the kitchen after the **steelworks** shut.
S2.quote: My dad was out of work for two years when the steelworks shut. I don't want to be sitting in the kitchen like my dad at thirty-two.
fieldNote: His father's unemployment after the **steelworks** closed shapes his fear more than any forecast.
He sees the 2028 thinking-AI wave hitting **supervisors**, leaving less slack for a slow junior.
He blames **choices** by government and owners, not the technology itself.
His only plan is **defensive**: savings, votes and Kasia's wage.

steps.text: Cut every non-essential cost and bank the difference before 2031
Vote for candidates promising a robot tax or job guarantees
Go to every union meeting and sign the petitions
Move in with Kasia's mother if one wage can't cover rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, really: the machines should pay their way and the workers should get a say in how it's done. I'd want the union to sit down with Northgate now, while there's time, and get something in writing about retraining and notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight years until the robots arrive, and I'd finally learn the press properly just in time for a robot to take the press off me. That's the cruel bit. I'd have time to get the warning off my name, and I'd still be under forty when it's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd do the forklift ticket and maybe a basic electrics course if the union pays for it, which they sometimes do. I'd keep the savings growing and not buy a car unless we had to. Around 2033 I'd start looking at warehouse or delivery work, anything still hands-on, before the press goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick than the fast one, more of a dull worry that sits there. Five years sounds a lot until you count how fast the last five went. I'd be anxious, but at least I'd feel like I was doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at warehouse work. Wouldn't robots reach warehouses too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah, I hadn't really thought that through. I suppose I'm just picking the next hands-on thing I can imagine. Maybe the electrics course matters more than the forklift then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want written down in that union agreement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months' notice before any press gets a robot, and the company paying for a course of your choosing. And no one over fifty-five pushed out without a proper payoff, for Dennis's sake. That's not a lot to ask from a firm that's saving millions.

say: I'd say the machines should **pay their way** and workers should have a say.
I'd want the union to get a **written deal** with Northgate while there's still time.
think: I think I'd finally get **good at the job** just as it's taken away.
Eight years to the robots is most of my **working life** before forty.
do: Get a **forklift licence** this year and a basic **electrics** course if the union pays.
Keep growing **savings** and avoid buying a car unless forced.
Start looking at other **hands-on work** around 2033, before the press goes.
feel: A **dull worry** that sits there, less sick than the fast picture.
Some comfort from feeling he's **doing something** at last.
S3.quote: Eight years until the robots arrive, and I'd finally learn the press properly just in time for a robot to take the press off me.
fieldNote: The cruelty for him is learning the trade **just in time** to lose it.
When challenged he admits warehouses aren't safe either and shifts toward **electrics**.
His union demands are specific: **six months' notice** and paid courses.
Extra time lets him **act**, which lowers his panic but not his worry.

steps.text: Take a forklift licence and a union-funded basic electrics course this year
Press the union for six months' notice and paid courses
Keep savings growing and put off buying a car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, there's time to do it properly this time, not like the steelworks. Ten years is enough for the government to set up real retraining and a proper safety net. I'd say that at the union, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years sounds like forever to me, and that's the trouble. I know myself, I'd do nothing until 2037 and then panic. I'd be forty by the time the robots come, which is old to start again but not too old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Northgate, get better at the press and stay in the union. I'd do the forklift ticket at some point, and I'd keep saving like we do. Mostly I'd wait and see which way it goes, because ten years is a long time and things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, honestly. It's far enough off that it feels like somebody else's problem, even though it's mine. There's still a little knot there, because forty with no trade isn't a great place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do nothing until 2037 and then panic. What would stop that happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kasia, probably, she's the planner of the two of us. If she put a date on the calendar for a course, I'd go. On my own I'd just keep turning up and hoping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the ten years change anything about your plans with Kasia, like where you live or having children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids in a few years, and ten years of notice doesn't really stop that. If anything it'd make me want to save harder before the baby, not after. Kids don't wait for robots.

say: I'd say ten years gives **time** to do it properly, not like the steelworks.
I'd want the government to build real **retraining** and a **safety net** in that time.
think: I know I'd probably do **nothing until 2037** and then panic.
At **forty** with no trade, starting again would be hard but not impossible.
do: Carry on at Northgate, getting better at the **press** and staying in the union.
Do the **forklift licence** at some point and keep saving as now.
Mostly **wait and see**, since ten years is a long time for things to change.
feel: **Calmer**, as if it's somebody else's problem.
A small **knot** about being forty with no trade.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds like forever to me, and that's the trouble. I know myself, I'd do nothing until 2037 and then panic.
fieldNote: He's frank that extra time feeds his **habit of waiting**, not his planning.
His girlfriend **Kasia** is the planner; she would decide when he trains.
He'd still plan **children** in a few years, saving harder first.

steps.text: Stay on the night press at Northgate and work on the scrap rate
Keep going to union meetings about the long-term plan
Wait to see how the decade plays out before choosing a course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no contest, because I'd have three years and no plan and no trade. What would help is the union having a deal ready before it happens, and a government that actually pays people while they learn something. Not a website with courses on it, a wage while you train.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about nights. Half the people on my shift are already worn out and half-ill from never seeing daylight. Whatever happens with robots, I'd like someone to remember that the people doing this job now are tired.

headlineQuote: Not a website with courses on it, a wage while you train.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old** night-shift moulding operator at **Northgate Plastics**, still on a scrap-rate warning.
He rents with care worker **Kasia**, with three months saved, and **rent** is his everyday worry.
He's a loyal **union** man who avoids screens and blames owners and government, not machines.
His fear grows with speed: **uneasy** in the plateau, **alarmed** when robots arrive by 2031.
Given ten years, he admits he'd simply **wait** until the last moment.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years until robots leaves him with no **trade** and no plan.
whatWouldHelp: A **union deal** in place beforehand and a **wage** while training, not just online courses.
